children: *China's Rising Aluminum Output Helps Keep Prices in Check Despite Middle East Supply Disruptions
*LME Aluminum Futures Hover Around $3,000 a Ton, Down 8% on-Month
*Chinese Aluminum Output, Indonesia's Production and Middle East Recovery Key Price Drivers in Near Term, Analysts Say
China's Rising Aluminum Output Cushions Gulf Supply Shock — Analysis
By Giulia Petroni
China's surging production and export of aluminum is offsetting war-related supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf, helping keep prices in check for one of the world's most widely used metals.

Chinese smelters have ramped up aluminum output over the past few months despite rising energy costs, buoyed by strong margins and cheaper raw-material costs as new refining capacity comes online, analysts said.

The expansion in China's production and export of aluminum comes as the war in the Middle East knocked out hundreds of thousands of tons in regional smelting capacity and blocked a vital supply waterway earlier this year. While China is the world's biggest producer of aluminum, metal makers in the Persian Gulf account for about a tenth of global output, raising fears of a severe supply gap due to the conflict.
"China has offset much of the shortfall elsewhere," said Barbara Lambrecht, commodity analyst at Commerzbank.

Beijing's aluminum exports rose 16% on year in the first eight months of 2026, an increase of around 670,000 metric tons, according to the U.S. Commerce Department's International Trade Administration. That additional volume helped partly offset a roughly 970,000-ton decline in exports from the United Arab Emirates, which is home to one of the biggest aluminum producers globally.

The surge in Chinese exports comes on the back of rising production. The country produced 3.91 million metric tons of primary aluminum in September, up 3.1% from a year earlier, according to data released Monday by the National Bureau of Statistics. Output in the first nine months of the year reached 35.03 million tons, an increase of 3.8% from the same period in 2025.
Meanwhile, a new refinery in the southern Chinese province of Guangxi is set to significantly expand output.

Rising Chinese supply has helped fill much of the gap left by the Gulf's production losses. Aluminum prices have eased as a result, returning close to levels seen in February, before the U.S.-Iran war began. Three-month aluminum futures on the London Metal Exchange traded around $3,000 a metric ton on Thursday, down 8% on the month. In early March, they had climbed to an intraday high of $4,073.50 a ton.

China isn't the only source of additional supply. Indonesia is expanding its refining and smelting industries as part of a push to process more raw materials domestically. Its aluminum production is projected to rise to 4 million tons in 2030 from 619,000 tons in 2025, while alumina output is expected to more than double to 9.1 million tons from 4.3 million tons, according to S&P Global.

With major Gulf producers still working to restore damaged facilities and establish alternative shipping routes, the balance between Chinese output, Indonesia's growing production, and the recovery in Middle Eastern supply is expected to remain a key driver of aluminum prices in the near term.

"The market should be loosening as Indonesia ramps up exports and Middle Eastern supply continues to recover," analysts at Morgan Stanley said. The U.S. bank projected last month a market surplus of more than 800,000 tons in 2027, with prices falling to $2,800 a ton.

In September, aluminum production across Gulf states was roughly 35% below prewar levels in February, according to the latest data from the International Aluminium Institute, an industry group representing producers accounting for about 60% of global output.

Iranian attacks in March forced Emirates Global Aluminium-owned by Mubadala, an Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund, and the government of Dubai--to shut its Al Taweelah facilities. The company said it has since restarted half of the smelter's production units and is targeting a return to full production in the first quarter of next year.

EGA is also seeking to diversify its export routes. At the end of September, it signed an agreement with logistics provider Gulftainer to expand aluminum shipments through the U.A.E.'s east coast, reducing reliance on traditional shipping routes disrupted by the conflict.

Aluminium Bahrain, operator of one of the world's largest aluminum smelters, also shut some production lines earlier this year. It has since used alternative export routes, including through Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Jeddah and Sohar in Oman, to bypass disrupted shipping lanes. The company said it is operating at about 80% of its prewar production capacity.

The recovery in Middle Eastern production appears to be progressing smoothly, according to market watchers. However, moving alumina into the region and shipping finished metal out remain potential bottlenecks, as supply chains remain exposed to renewed disruptions.

China, meanwhile, has an annual capacity ceiling of 45 million tons. The government-imposed cap, introduced in 2017 to tackle oversupply and reduce emissions during a period of rapid expansion in the industry, applies to installed smelting capacity rather than actual annual production.

If aluminum prices fall further and the market moves into a sustained surplus, Beijing could enforce the cap even more strictly, potentially limiting the industry's ability to expand output in the future, Commerzbank's Lambrecht said.

Chinese producers are also increasingly looking overseas for growth, with investments in smelting capacity in countries such as Indonesia or Kazakhstan to expand production beyond domestic constraints.
